title: Training progression and exercise setup
body:
The most useful habit in this coaching period was keeping the exercise setup consistent before judging whether a lift had improved. For barbell movements, record the stance, grip and range of motion beside the load. For machines, keep a note of the seat setting and the equipment used. Alex's training became easier to review when a repeated exercise meant a repeated movement, rather than simply the same name in the log. A heavier machine-stack reading was treated as a new reference when the equipment changed, rather than compared directly with an earlier machine.

The growth-phase sessions worked best when the first working set was recorded carefully and the later sets followed the same technique. We reviewed the load, the completed repetitions and the reported effort together. The aim was to understand the performance rather than chase a larger number at every session. A set performed with a shorter range of motion was discussed in the check-in instead of automatically treated as evidence of better strength. These distinctions made the personal-best table more useful when looking back through the training period.

The upper/lower schedule also became easier to sustain when exercise order stayed familiar. Alex knew which movement mattered most in each session and could compare the opening working sets with the previous week. Accessories were easier to adjust around a busy day because the main session structure was already clear. When a different gym was used, Alex recorded the substitution in the notes so that the following review did not confuse a change of equipment with a change of performance. The coach & athlete review focused on patterns across several sessions.

During prep, the same log remained useful even when loads did not increase. A completed session with consistent execution helped us see that the plan was still manageable. Where performance fell across several exercises at once, the next discussion considered the wider check-in rather than one disappointing set. This is an observation from the sample coaching period, rather than a rule that every future training block must follow. It should be read alongside the dated weigh-ins, recovery notes and the actual training record.

For the next coach, the most useful starting point is a conversation about which movements Alex wants to keep and which setups can still be reproduced. The personal-best entries show what was logged, but the surrounding notes explain the circumstances. Keep the machine details, exercise order and any substitutions beside the numbers. That context will make future comparisons fairer and preserve the practical lessons from this coaching period without requiring the next coach to copy every part of the old plan.

One example was the way Alex recorded dumbbell work after changing gyms. The available increments were different, so an increase in the written load did not always mean the planned progression had happened in the same way. The accompanying note explained the change and helped the coach compare the next few sessions more carefully. Keeping that explanation beside the numbers was more useful than removing it to make the training log look tidy. The next review could then use the new equipment as its reference without losing the earlier record.

The longer comments also captured Alex's preferences about the session itself. Alex found it helpful to know the priority exercise before arriving at the gym and preferred a clear explanation when the order changed. When a session was shortened, the log named the work that was completed and the reason for the change. These are small practical details, but together they explain why one version of the plan was easier to follow than another. Keeping the full note in this handover gives the next coach that context rather than only a list of the best numbers.

title: Upper-body sessions
body:
The most consistent upper-body sessions started with the main press while Alex was fresh, followed by the main row. Keeping those movements early made week-to-week comparisons easier. The incline dumbbell press was recorded as the weight of one dumbbell, not the combined pair. That convention should remain visible wherever those records are displayed.

Alex preferred to keep the accessory choices familiar for several weeks rather than replace them after one difficult session. The coach noted better session completion when the written plan was easy to follow and the expected equipment was available. During travel weeks, the exercise notes named the substitute machine so the later review could treat it as a separate reference. This is useful context for choosing the next block, rather than a requirement to keep the same exercises indefinitely.

title: Lower-body sessions
body:
Alternating the main squat session and the main hinge session across the week gave the lower-body plan a clear structure. Alex found it easier to prepare for each session when the priority movement was obvious. The written plan also made it clearer which accessory work could move when a session had to be shortened.

The coach's most useful observations came from several sessions together: attendance, completed sets and Alex's description of recovery. A single good or difficult day did not tell the whole story. When a gym change affected the available leg-curl machine, the log recorded the equipment difference. The sample personal best is therefore a record on the machine used at the time. The next coach should check the current equipment before using it as a direct comparison.

title: Growth-phase review
body:
The sample growth-phase target was approximately +0.5 kg per week. The coach reviewed that historical target alongside the rolling seven-day bodyweight average and the training log. Individual weigh-ins moved up and down, so the discussion focused on the direction across recorded readings rather than reacting to every daily change.

The most useful check-ins included a short explanation of anything unusual in that week, such as travel or a different weigh-in routine. Alex's recorded gain was generally close to the target while training performance improved. This note preserves the target used and the coach's assessment of that period; it does not set an automatic target for the future. The next phase should be discussed using the client's current goals and circumstances, rather than assuming the previous growth phase should simply be repeated.

title: Weigh-in consistency
body:
Alex's bodyweight record was easiest to interpret when the weigh-in routine was consistent and any changes to that routine were mentioned in the check-in. The trend used recorded readings only. A missing reading stayed missing, and the reading count remained visible alongside the rolling seven-day average.

For future reviews, keep the distinction between a milestone and a trend clear. Peak bulk, the actual pre-prep reading and the show-day reading are individual dated observations. The trend is an average of the available readings in each seven-day window. Both are useful, but they answer different questions. Where a milestone has not been recorded, the report should say Not recorded instead of choosing a nearby number or a planned target and presenting it as an actual result.

title: Prep and show-day context
body:
The sample pre-prep bodyweight was recorded on 01 June, and the actual show-day bodyweight was recorded on 27 September. Those dates give the two values their meaning. A target entered before the competition is separate from the weight actually observed on the day and should not replace it in the handover.

During the later part of prep, Alex's check-in comments helped explain the training record. The most useful notes described the completed sessions and how manageable the week felt, rather than reporting bodyweight alone. For the next coach, these comments provide context for the period around the show. They are a record of what happened in this fictional example, not instructions for a future prep or a reason to reproduce the same changes without a fresh review.

title: Sleep and routine
body:
The coach noted that Alex found the training week easier to manage when the sleep routine was more predictable. The most useful check-ins described changes to the normal schedule rather than providing a number without context. That gave the coach a better picture of a difficult week and helped explain why an individual session might feel different.

When reviewing this period, keep the recorded observation separate from a promise about future results. The note records that Alex reported better recovery during weeks with a steadier routine. It does not prove that one habit explains every performance change. The next coach can use this as a conversation starter and compare it with the client's current routine, preferences and logged experience.

title: Lower-volume weeks
body:
The sample coach used lower-volume weeks when the wider training and recovery picture suggested that the normal week was becoming harder to manage. The relevant check-ins described more than a single missed repetition. They included how several sessions had gone and Alex's own account of recovery.

The handover should preserve the coach's reasoning as well as the adjustment. In this example, Alex reported better training quality after the easier week. Recording the period and the response makes that observation easier to discuss later. It should not become an automatic calendar rule or an instruction to repeat exactly the same adjustment. The next coach can decide whether the earlier pattern is still relevant after reviewing the current training record.

title: Check-ins and communication
body:
The most useful check-ins were short enough to complete consistently but specific enough to explain the week. Alex usually mentioned the sessions that went well, any substitutions, and one practical issue that affected the plan. That made it easier for the coach to respond with a clear change or a reason to keep the plan steady.

Longer notes were helpful when there was more context to preserve, particularly around travel, a change of gym, or the period near the show. Those details should remain readable in the handover rather than cut off to fit a fixed box. The next coach can use them to understand Alex's preferences and communication style, while agreeing their own check-in process at the start of the next coaching relationship.

title: Context for the next coach
body:
Alex valued a clear weekly structure, familiar exercise names and explanations for changes. The strongest parts of the sample coaching record were the consistent training log and the comments that explained why a week differed from the usual routine. The milestone bodyweights and personal-best sets are useful reference points, but the notes help explain the experience behind them.

At the next review, discuss which parts of the previous plan Alex wants to keep and which need to change. Check that the equipment and exercise setups still match the recorded lifts before comparing numbers. Where the report says Not recorded, leave that gap visible rather than filling it with an assumption. These notes are a handover of the sample coaching period, with room for the next coach to build a plan around current goals.
